claims.text: The baseline as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating has a relatively coarse, unrefined grain structure.
A controlled high-temperature annealing or pre-conditioning step will promote dynamic surface nanocrystallization in FeNiCrCoCu coatings.
Thermal activation during high-temperature sliding aids dynamic recrystallization during deformation.
Dynamic recrystallization or amorphization forms an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer during sliding.
The ultra-nanocrystalline layer contains a refined, high-density grain-boundary network.
Nanocrystallization in the inverse Hall-Petch regime reduces local shear strength.
Formation of the ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer lowers friction in FeNiCrCoCu coatings.
The refined near-surface structure improves the coating's ability to accommodate deformation.
Formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer reduces wear.
The ultra-nanocrystalline layer resists crack initiation.
The annealed coating will have a lower wear rate than the as-deposited control under otherwise identical high-temperature sliding conditions.
The annealed coating will exhibit finer surface grains than the as-deposited control after sliding.
The annealed coating will exhibit less microscopic crack formation than the as-deposited control.
The as-deposited control lacks significant dynamic surface nanocrystallization.
The proposed wear-resistance enhancement will hold primarily during high-temperature sliding.
The effect may differ at lower temperatures or under non-sliding conditions.

contradictions.description: The intervention implies that pre-sliding annealing itself produces or promotes nanocrystallization, whereas the conditions and mediator attribute formation of the layer to a dynamic process occurring during sliding deformation. The timing and causal role of annealing versus sliding are not resolved.

Dynamic recrystallization and amorphization are presented interchangeably as the origin of an ultra-nanocrystalline layer, although they describe different structural transformations and no sequence connecting them is specified.

The hypothesis separately predicts reduced wear and changed deformation, but the falsification rule requires both no wear reduction and no nanocrystalline layer. Thus, failure of either central prediction alone would not falsify the hypothesis under the stated rule.
